To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
real assisted passenger fares on the sailing vessel trade to Australia were procyclical, and were procyclical to a lesser degree on the homeward leg than on the outward leg.
the real fares were lower on the homeward legs, that they varied with the number of assisted immigrants, and that the seasonality was not significant.

the real fares on assisted passages to Australia varied with the number of assisted migrants embarked, the season of the year, and the number of passengers on the homeward leg, but not with total demand, or relative demand on the outbound leg.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a consistent series of passenger fares on sailing ships to Australia from the UK in the nineteenth century and the statistical analysis of the fares.

the following issues: (1) the relationship between passenger fares and freight rates, (2) the relationship between the real fares and the variables measuring the demand for shipping space on the outward and return legs, (3) the relationship between real fares and the number of assisted migrants, (4) the relationship between fares and the season of departure, (5) the effect of the joint production of space and the characteristics of a voyage on fares, (6) the effect of freight rates and freight subsidies

the construction and analysis of a consistent series of passenger fares on sailing ships to Australia from the UK in the nineteenth century, with particular attention being given to the joint production characteristics that apply to a voyage, and to the general characteristics of the Europe-Far East trade.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the fares were not determined by supply and demand in the sense of a competitive market, but were rather determined by the joint production characteristics and the general characteristics mentioned above.
the assisted fares were not a simple reflection of the cost of shipping space.
the assisted passenger fares were not determined solely by the demand for shipping space on the homeward leg of the voyage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the passenger fares were not determined solely by the demand and supply of shipping space, but were influenced by the number of passengers and the season of voyage.
the real assisted fares on sailing vessels from the United Kingdom to Australia were not significantly different from the fares on sailing vessels in the general Europe-Far East trade.

the passenger fares on sailing vessel voyages to Australia were not determined by a single set of market forces, but by a complex set of market forces which varied with the season of the year, the number of passengers embarked and the number of passengers carried on the homeward leg.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the real fares on sailing vessels were not as volatile as the nominal fares suggest.

the assisted passenger fares on the homeward legs were lower than the fares on the outward legs, but the difference in fares was not sufficient to compensate for the difference in the number of assisted migrants on the two legs.

the fares on sailing vessels were not a pure monopoly price, but rather were a price which reflected the costs of providing a voyage and the relative demand for shipping space on the outward and return legs.
